articles.title: Commonwealth medallist Lobban switches from Scotland to Australia
articles.summary: Scottish-born squash player Greg Lobban will represent Australia for the first time at this week's China Open.
articles.body:
Scottish-born squash player Greg Lobban will represent Australia for the first time at this week's China Open.

The 34-year-old, who was born in Inverness and has represented Scotland at three Commonwealth Games, confirmed his Australian citizenship had been approved on Tuesday, saying he will now "get to play under the Australian flag".

Lobban won a doubles bronze medal for Scotland at the 2022 Commonwealth Games and has 16 PSA titles to his name.

The news is therefore a blow to Scottish squash but does not come as a surprise.

In an interview with BBC Scotland in June, the world number 29 confirmed he was in the process of applying for citizenship in Australia and believed it was "the best decision for me and my family".

Lobban, who has an Australian wife, added that the lure of potentially playing at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles - where the sport will make its Games debut - hastened an already planned move.

"I have got strong Australian ties with my wife being born there and my son being half Australian, so this was going to happen at some point," he said.

"I was thinking it was probably going to be post-squash career in terms of applying for residency and citizenship, but the prospect of representing Australia at the Olympics is too much of an exciting opportunity to turn down.

"At this stage of my career, this is really motivation to put in a good two years and hopefully be able to have Australian representation at the Games."

articles.title: La natación española sale a flote
articles.standfirst: Un abanico de nadadores interesantes rodean al contrastado Hugo González. Los inminentes Mundiales de Pekín en piscina corta serán un buen test
articles.summary: Un abanico de nadadores interesantes rodean al contrastado Hugo González. Los inminentes Mundiales de Pekín en piscina corta serán un buen test
articles.body: Pocos deportes en España han transitado su historia internacional por un desfiladero tan estrecho como la natación, donde el talento ha brotado con cuentagotas y cada generación ha tenido casi siempre un único referente al que mirar. A Martin López Zubero, le sucedieron Sergi López, el hermano del primero, David y Nina Zhivaneskaia para desembocar en Mireia Belmonte, la más laureada de todos los mencionados. De pronto apareció Hugo González, un campeón mundial contrastado que aún persigue una medalla olímpica, y parecía que la raquítica hilera avanzaría un periodo más, pero sorprendentemente la última generación que ha surgido hace mirar con optimismo Los Ángeles 2028, el horizonte que fijó Sean Kelley, el antiguo director técnico, cuando tomó las riendas de la natación española tras Tokio 2020. Los Europeos de París del año pasado, el título de 200 braza mundial logrado por un superespecialista en piscina de 25 metros, Carles Coll, en 2024 y los resultados de los Campeonatos de España de la semana pasada han provocado un estado de cierto optimismo que pasa no tantos por los podios, que podría haberlos, como que las tardes de las grandes competiciones tengan banderas españolas en alguna de las ocho calles de las finales. Además de Hugo, que arrojó la segunda mejor marca de 2026 en 200 espalda, es muy valorable lo que aportan Luca Hoek, el velocista más rápido que ha tenido este país, y su compañero de entrenamientos Miguel Pérez-Godoy, ilusionantes si César Castro llega fino a Pekín en dos semanas como el cuarto relevista del 4x200. En un deporte en el que se trabajaba de forma poco transversal, con tipos tan brillantes y tan particulares al mismo tiempo como Fred Vergnoux, ahora parece haber una comunión más clara entre Titley, Greenwood, Navalón... También el sector femenino parece tener una estrella emergente en Irene Ciércoles. Tiene 16 años y es una nadadora por hacer. Pero cada vez que se tira a la piscina, tiembla una plusmarca nacional. Los próximos Mundiales en piscina olímpica de este verano en Budapest se antojan el gran termómetro del estado real de la natación. Pero, de momento, este deporte ha vuelto a los titulares.

articles.title: Josh Kerr: The Making of the Man Behind the Shades
articles.summary: People know Josh Kerr the athlete. But are there two Josh Kerrs? The mile world record holder talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, 4am kebabs in Paris, entering races under a false name and his granny keeping him humble.
articles.body:
The guy with the shades. The fastest man to ever run a mile. Scottish, but with a curious transatlantic accent. Slicked-back hair. Beard. Usually got a medal of some kind slung around his neck. No stranger to telling you what he thinks.

That's Kerr the competitor, one of the foremost faces in world athletics, and a man who rampaged around London's Olympic Stadium in three minutes 42.66 seconds in July to set a new world record. Then followed it up with a home Commonwealth gold and an imperious triumph at the Ultimate Championship.

Kerr recognises the description, smiling as it's articulated. But is there another version of him? Speaking to him during one of his regular returns to Scotland from his New Mexico base, it becomes clear there is.

There's scant chat about records, medals and his enjoyably-niggly rivalry with Jakob Ingebrigtsen.

Instead, he talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, 4am kebabs in Paris, entering races under a false name, cold-calling universities, being starstruck meeting Scotland's rugby players and his granny keeping him humble.

This is the Kerr who spent the thick end of an hour on a chilly August evening taking selfies, signing his name, and sharing his wisdom with young fans at Scotstoun after his Commonwealth medal presentation.

The Kerr who is still a regular visitor to first club Edinburgh AC's training sessions. This is Uncle Josh, who is heading for a party with his nephews after this chat.

The difference between the two versions of Kerr? The shades...

"They really help me switch my personality into work mode," he tells BBC Sport. "I think everyone has a work persona and it's a bit more intensified when it comes to my sport.

"Not a lot of things matter when I'm focused on my job, but the rest of the 23 hours and 56-and-a-bit minutes of the day, it's very different."

Josh Kerr: The Making of the Man Behind the Shades

'My brother still thinks he can beat me... that's the Kerr delusion'

Kerr is sitting in the bay window of his parents' dining room as the autumnal gloom gathers in this desirable part of Edinburgh. All grand facades, imposing trees and permit parking.

His granny lives at the end of the road. His brother Jake and his family are 20 minutes outside the city. His school – the prestigious George Watson's – is a mile away.

The house has been home since Josh was five months old. Even now, this is where he returns on his five or six trips back to Scotland each year from his Albuquerque base, albeit the "chaos" of his teenage bedroom has long since been vanquished.

"It brings all different sorts of emotions," Kerr says of walking back through the terraced property's teal front door at the start of each visit. "As a kid, I would train from here every day. Everything started from that door.

"It's nice to fall back into that routine when I'm here. I can see the splits I'm running in my loops versus when I was 15. Slightly quicker..."

Around him in the room, pictures of the two brothers fight for space with memorabilia from their careers and assorted artwork. Jake - like their father John - was a professional rugby player, earning a cap for Scotland in the 2019 Six Nations.

He is 18 months older so served as not just an example to follow, but also a target to catch when Josh started racing at the age of nine, having caught the eye at a summer camp.

"If anyone ever wants to nerd out on the family stats, Jake has a pretty awesome under-15 cross-country record," Kerr says.

"We raced a couple of times, once at the Scottish cross-country relays when I ran under someone else's name because they didn't turn up, which was very hush-hush. I just followed him around, holding on for dear life.

"He still likes to remind me that I've never had an unbeaten season and he has. He still thinks he can beat me. That's the solid Kerr delusion in him. But it got me this far, so I can't question it."

The 29-year-old hasn't always had that familial brashness, though.

Dad John says "you wouldn't believe how quiet he was" as a child, speculating that Jake did his talking for him. And mum Jill – who has a background in tennis and is now her son's lead physio – recalls his "kindness and emotional intelligence".

Like all good parents, they are also a source of more esoteric anecdotes. Jill remembers providing both boys breakfasts in bed on competition days and teasing Josh for his "showboating", while John reveals that the teenager turned up to parties with non-alcoholic booze or arrived home sweating if he did have a beer, having run all the way back.

"Those are pretty niche stories," Kerr says, perhaps making a mental note to clamp his father later. "Everyone was starting to get into beers and things like that but it was just not really my thing. I found you could just rip the non-alcoholic bit off the label and get on with the socialising."

By the stage, any ambitions of following his dad and brother into rugby – as a full-back in his case - had been shelved, and his attention focused on athletics.

Kerr "wasn't a phenom by any means" and recalls winning races only "now and again", but the quiet kid had developed a resolve that running would be his future.

"Someone's got to be the best in the world, so why not me? That's what I had in my head," he explains. "I wanted to be a pro athlete and I knew running was going to be my ticket to that. The next stage for me was to go university and get that paid for."

The problem was his athletic record, while good, wasn't stellar. And neither were his academic grades. Kerr needed to hustle.

He enlisted the help of his parents – and fellow Edinburgh AC luminary Chris O'Hare – to compile a list of US colleges and compose a CV and cover letter, then set about selling himself.

"I was 16 and just whipping emails out, left, right and centre, saying 'hey, I'm coming over in 2015, do you have a spot for me?' And it was a pretty big no across the board," says Kerr, who re-read all the rejection emails recently.

"Then New Mexico said 'we'll take you' and I was like, 'perfect, I'll be there'. I told my parents and their first question was 'are they going to pay your fees?' and I was like 'uhm, well, I didn't ask'. So they made me phone back and check!"

He did and they were, which set in motion the move that would change Kerr's life in more ways than one.

It was on his first week in Albuquerque, while on a campus bus that his parents blagged their way on to posing as professors, that Kerr met Larimar Rodriguez, who became his wife last year.

"It was a big week," he says. "It's one of those ones where you don't really realise until you look back.

"I met Larimar when I was 17 and I'm incredibly proud of her. She's done four years of undergrad, four years of med school, and now she's in her fourth year of residency. She'll be a full attending dermatologist by June or July."

Saturday scrap ends with emotional Kerr winning fight

Selfies, signatures & social media - how Kerr embraced Glasgow Games

Britain's Kerr breaks 27-year mile world record in London

'I got recognised at the end of the street... it was my granny'

Josh and Larimar live together in New Mexico with their mini schnauzer El Presidente, who often joins Kerr on his lighter runs.

That's part of a precisely-honed routine that starts with alternate ice baths and hot tub dips at 5am, and some visualisation and journaling around breakfast before he "goes to work" at the track or in the gym from 10am-2pm.

The next three hours are spent in his bedroom, which has been adapted to serve as an altitude chamber, before he retires for the day before 9pm.

The attention to detail is startling. Childhood friend and fellow former world 1500m champion Jake Wightman recounts sharing a room with bronze medallist Kerr at the Tokyo Olympics and looking on in bemusement as he unpacked a scented diffuser, mattress topper and waffle maker to replicate being at home.

Five years on, Kerr has a team of 16 in his Brooks Beast running family under head coach Danny Mackey, including personal chef Jameel, a mental performance consultant and a chiropractor.

It's a long way from life behind that teal door in Edinburgh but how different is Kerr now from the one who left his homeland 11 years ago? "Pretty similar," he says, while acknowledging that he is now more outwardly confident of his abilities.

That "abrasive, calling-your-shot side" as he calls it, is not a traditional trait for a Scot but has been shaped by more than a decade in the United States and by his desire to shine a light on athletics.

"Everyone says, 'oh, we're not getting attention' but go out and earn it," Kerr says. "Make people want to care about what you're doing.

"I'm an individual business and I'm trying as hard as I can to bring eyeballs because I think athletics is the purest form of sport. It didn't really come naturally to me before - being in the US has kind of shaped me a little bit – but I hope people realise that the reason I'm in this position is the blood that runs through my veins.

"I'm able to represent the UK a lot more than I'm able to represent Scotland, but it's such a huge part of who I am. And I hope they take great pride in the performances I'm able to produce.

"I've been inspired by some incredible athletes and I guess this is my turn to step up and try and bridge the gap between grassroots and where I'm at."

Kerr has done that on the track, with two Olympic medals to add to his world indoor and outdoor golds, but he is approaching a stage where his celebrity might breach the confines of athletics.

Take last week. On a four-day visit home, his duties as Uncle Josh were surrounded by a glut of sponsorship and media engagements – including an appearance on the BBC's flagship current affairs programme Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg - as well as a coaching session with young athletes and an invite to carry out the match ball at Murrayfield before Scotland faced New Zealand.

Of course, the omnipresent spectre of BBC Sports Personality of the Year is looming into view, too. Kerr, it should be noted, is not shy in coveting that prize.

That he will likely be one of the main contenders speaks to how life has changed for him in the past couple of years.

Kerr can still enjoy being back in Edinburgh in relative peace - "I got recognised at the end of the street recently… it was my granny" – but concedes life in America can be a bit more challenge because of requests for "400 selfies and a video for their nan".

That attention will only intensify over the coming months should he complete the one or two outstanding items on his athletics tick list and frank his ambition of being "remembered as the best middle-distance athlete of all time".

While he is waiting to see how his winter training goes before 'calling his shot' again, Kerr has other world records in his sights and, of course, Los Angeles in 2028 and a chance to complete the full set of Olympic medals by winning gold.

Silver was not what he wanted in Paris - albeit the passing of time has allowed some satisfaction with the British record he ran – so righting that wrong in the States is top of his agenda.

Kerr has already made a low-key visit to the Colosseum, the epic venue two hours from his New Mexico home where the athletics events will be staged, to help visualise the moment – just as he did with the Stade de France.

He will be back again before the shades go on and he gets down to the business of proving himself to be the best ever.

articles.title: 'You cannot be a champion without working like one': Vivaan Kapoor on his Doha silver, Olympic dream
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: For shooter Vivaan Kapoor, winning a silver medal at the World Championships in Doha in the men's trap event was not just a reward for his hard
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For shooter Vivaan Kapoor, winning a silver medal at the World Championships in Doha in the men's trap event was not just a reward for his hard work but also a reminder of how far he has come in a sport where one missed target can change everything. Having secured an Olympic quota for India, the young shooter is now focused on maintaining his form, making the most of the opportunities ahead and continuing his journey towards the biggest stage in sport."It was not easy because it was a very windy time when we went there. There were a lot of gusts of wind and even the second day was very gloomy. In shooting, especially in my event, it really matters whether it is cloudy or sunny because that depends on how you see the target," Kapoor said.However, he believes that dealing with such challenges is part of an athlete's preparation. "Wind is generally the toughest thing to keep control of. But in the end, it was the same for everybody. We train to be in such conditions and perform even when things are tough," he said.While technical ability remains central to shooting, Kapoor believes the mental side of the sport is what separates the best from the rest. With several shots to negotiate in quick succession, the ability to move on from a mistake can be the difference between a medal and a disappointing finish.For Kapoor, the key word is 'reset'."You cannot be a superhuman or a robot. It is normal to feel bad after missing a target. I tell myself, 'Okay, Vivaan, you are feeling bad about it. See what you did, try not to make that mistake the next time and move forward.' You don't have much time before your next shot, so you cannot get into a deep analysis. You have to understand the mistake and move on," he explained.He believes that champions are often distinguished by how quickly they can put a bad shot behind them rather than by whether they experience disappointment at all.Kapoor's recent progress has also been shaped by technical changes. Around six months ago, he decided to change his personal coach and began working with Croatian shooter Giovanni Cernogoraz, an Olympic gold medallist."The changes were made collectively by my personal coach and national coach. Peter Wilson helped me change my stance, while my stock was also changed. There were a few things related to my movement towards the target that we worked on. Making these changes in such a short time before the World Championships was challenging, but when you make the right changes, things start going up," he said.The 24-year-old also credited the changing atmosphere within the Indian shooting camp for the country's growing success on the international stage. He believes Wilson has brought a different mindset to the team, encouraging shooters to embrace pressure rather than be overwhelmed by it."I think 65 per cent of this sport is mental, and the biggest change has been the mental approach brought in by Peter Wilson. The enthusiasm he brings is unbelievable. We did not have anybody with us who had such great ambitions for the country. He teaches us to shout 'India' loudly in the hotel. Earlier, we were shy about these things," Kapoor said.He added that the emphasis was now on believing that Indian shooters could dominate at the highest level."You can crumble under pressure or embrace it as a privilege. You can tell yourself that this is why you are here and why you do this sport for a living. That change in mood and mentality has been a big thing for us."Kapoor's own journey into shooting began through his father, who would occasionally visit shooting ranges with his friends. Although there were no shooters in his family, the stories he heard at home sparked an early fascination with firearms.Professionally, he drew inspiration from several coaches and accomplished shooters. He particularly remembers former coach Mansher Singh for instilling discipline during his formative years and Khalid Al-Mudaf for helping him develop the mental side of the sport. He also spoke warmly about Kainan, whom he considers an important influence in his development.However, it is his current coach Cernogoraz's work ethic that has left a lasting impression."He is somebody I look up to in terms of working hard. I realised that you cannot be a champion without working like a champion. I am fortunate to see how he works, from morning to evening at the range, and then comes back and runs 10 kilometres. When you see someone like that, it motivates you," Kapoor said.With the Los Angeles Olympics now on the horizon, Kapoor is keen to keep his feet on the ground. While his performance in Doha secured an Olympic quota place for India, it does not automatically guarantee him a place in the final team. The country's selection process will involve domestic trials, making the coming competitions equally important."By God's grace, I have the points and I am going to follow a plan that I had already made," he said.He is now looking forward to domestic competitions before assessing his international schedule and possible World Cup appearances.For a shooter who has learnt to put a missed target behind him and focus on the next one, the approach towards Los Angeles remains much the same. There is no room to dwell on what could have been in Doha or get carried away by what lies ahead. As Kapoor puts it, his job is to pick up his gun every day, give his best and enjoy the sport.And perhaps that is the mindset that will define the next chapter of his journey — one target at a time, with Los Angeles firmly in sight.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Athletics 2026 Season In Review: Andy Ibañez
articles.summary: Ibanez, we hardly knew you
articles.body:
It's that time of the year again! Athletics Nation is set to begin our annual Player Review Series. We'll be taking a look back at all the different players that suited up for the Green & Gold this year. Some were major contributors while others barely made any impact. Either way, we'll take a look back at the guys that made up the 2026 Athletics. We kick things off with infielder Andy Ibañez, who made the Opening Day roster after a late addition but wouldn't last long with the organization.

The Athletics claimed Ibañez off of waivers from the Los Angeles Dodgers on February 6th, less than a week before pitchers and catchers were due to report. Los Angeles had given Ibañez a relatively large $1.2 million contract earlier in the offseason with the hope that his salary would be too much to stomach for a claiming team. Since he was out of options, if Los Angeles decided to try to sneak him through waivers they could lose him to another team if that team were willing to take on that contract. Los Angeles went that route, trying to stash him in the minors as an expensive backup. The A's called the Dodgers' bluff and added him to the roster, along with the $1.2 million to the payroll.

The former Cuba defector has been around for a few years now. Ibañez made his big league debut in 2021 for the Texas Rangers at the age of 28. The right-handed hitter had a solid rookie campaign but would find himself in Detroit less than two years later. Those three years he spent with the Tigers were also productive as he was a multi-positional Swiss army knife for two playoff teams.

Still, it's not like he was lighting up the world on fire in the batter's box after slashing .239/.301/.352 in his final year in Detroit. Mostly a second and third baseman, the hope when the A's added him to the roster was that he could act as a safeguard at two questionable positions, primarily third base. Max Muncy was about to begin his first full season as a big leaguer at the hot corner and Ibañez could be the veteran fallback option if the former first-rounder couldn't figure it out. He wouldn't provide much upside, but even league-average production would be an upgrade over the previous year.

While Ibañez managed to hold onto a roster spot for the first 28 games, he only ended up getting into 11 of those contests for the Green & Gold with 18 plate appearances. He didn't make the most of those at bats as he collected just two singles and a walk. It wasn't what the A's were looking for, and with Muncy getting everyday at bats at the hot corner the A's elected to designate Ibañez for assignment on April 26th.

He was claimed off waivers by the New York Mets a few days later, taking on the remainder of his salary for the year. That was nice for the A's to get out of that contract. Ibañez made it into three games for New York but then spent the rest of the year in the minors, mostly with the Mets' Triple-A affiliate and then a brief stint in Seattle's system to end the year. Overall he went just two-for-23 in the big leagues this year while slashing .291/.325/.425 with 7 home runs in the minors.

Ibañez now finds himself back on the free agent market after electing free agency on November 2nd. He'll have to settle for a minor league deal wherever he can get one, but with his versatility on defense he should be able to find someone who would be interested in a depth piece like him. It just likely won't be the A's.

And so it begins. We'll be continuing our Player Review Series tomorrow!

articles.title: Sudáfrica pide disculpas a su mayor leyenda olímpica que competirá por Países Bajos: "Si pudiera, los despediría a todos"
articles.standfirst: El ministro de Deportes abrirá una investigación de las causas que han llevado a la nadadora Tatjana Smith a defender la bandera del país europeo del que también tiene la nacionalidad
articles.summary: El ministro de Deportes abrirá una investigación de las causas que han llevado a la nadadora Tatjana Smith a defender la bandera del país europeo del que también tiene la nacionalidad
articles.body: El ministro de Deportes de Sudáfrica, Gayton McKenzie, ordenó abrir una investigación sobre el trato recibido a la doble campeona olímpica de natación Tatjana Smith, quien anunció recientemente que competirá bajo la bandera de Países Bajos tras denunciar reiterados conflictos con la federación sudafricana. La decisión llegó después de quejas contra los dirigentes de Natación Sudáfrica por retenerle durante doce meses 35.000 dólares en premios que ganó en el Mundial de Natación de Fukuoka (Japón) en 2023. Según recogen medios locales este miércoles, la nadador denunció que el organismo le abonó la suma un año después sin los intereses correspondientes, los cuales solo cobró tras recurrir a sus abogados. El ministro McKenzie pidió disculpas públicas a la nadadora durante una rueda de prensa por el maltrato institucional al considerar: "la han tratado de la peor manera posible. Deberían sentir vergüenza. A Tatjana la han tratado como a una enemiga de este país", añadió. El titular de Deportes solicitó formalmente a la Confederación Deportiva y Comité Olímpico Sudafricano (SASCOC) que inicie una pesquisa contra los directivos de la federación nacional. "Si pudiera, saldría ahí mismo y los despediría a todos de inmediato. Así es como me siento", sumó el funcionario, aunque aclaró que una intervención directa del Gobierno acarrearía una suspensión internacional por parte de World Aquatics —la federación internacional de natación reconocida por el Comité Olímpico Internacional (COI)— y que la ley exige que el caso pase primero por SASCOC. "Si así es como tratan a la mayor deportista olímpica de nuestra historia, ¿cómo estamos tratando a nuestras estrellas emergentes? ¿Qué mensaje le envía todo esto a cada joven nadador sobre lo que puede esperar si nada cambia?", cerró McKenzie. Smith —quien compitió bajo su apellido de soltera, Schoenmaker, antes de contraer matrimonio— posee doble nacionalidad y es la deportista olímpica más laureada en la historia de Sudáfrica con cuatro medallas (dos de oro y dos de plata). La campeona se había retirado en 2024, pero este año revirtió su decisión con la mira puesta en los Juegos Olímpicos de Los Ángeles 2028. Tras conquistar el oro en los 200 metros braza en Tokio 2020 y en los 100 metros braza en París 2024, la nadadora buscará ahora el título en los 50 metros braza representando a Países Bajos. "Para Sudáfrica: cuando era niña, mi mayor sueño era representar a mi país en los Juegos Olímpicos. Pude vivir ese sueño y me dio más de lo que jamás hubiera imaginado", expresó Smith entre lágrimas en un video publicado este mes en sus redes sociales para comunicar su cambio de federación. La nadadora agregó que competir por el equipo neerlandés le permite "explorar otra parte" de su identidad y herencia familiar, además de ofrecerle "un mayor respaldo de alto rendimiento y la posibilidad de construir una carrera más sostenible".

articles.title: Luke Carson: Rhys McClenaghan's coach steps back from high performance role
articles.summary: Luke Carson, who helped guide Rhys McClenaghan to Olympic gold in 2024, has stepped away from high performance coaching.
articles.body:
Luke Carson, who helped guide Rhys McClenaghan to Olympic gold in 2024, has stepped away from high performance coaching.

It brings an end to one of the most successful athlete-coach partnerships in the history of Irish sport after 12 years together.

Carson, a former gymnast, helped assist McClenaghan to Olympic gold on the pommel horse at the 2024 Games in Paris in what was Ireland's first gymnastics medal.

Together, they completed gymnastics' 'Grand Slam'. McClenaghan, 27, also won back-to-back World Championship golds, as well as three European and a Commonwealth title on top of their Olympic success.

Carson has parted company with Gymnastics Ireland, where he was high performance coach and in charge of the Olympic programme for the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.

After meeting McClenaghan as a teenager in 2014, Carson said he had "raw talent" and they immediately had a "common understanding" that they would leave "no stone unturned".

Carson explained: "I guess our strategy was to do so much volume it would be unreasonable not to succeed.

"Rhys and I developed a uniquely wonderful dynamic, which was built on mutual respect for one another and for the sport itself.

"By almost every definition we were trailblazers. There was no established system for us to follow, no blueprint to copy, no history of results to soak in.

"Instead we had to create them. We had to dream things that never were."

McClenaghan wins pommel horse gold at Olympics

McClenaghan 2.0 'a work in progress' after injuries

Carson started working with a teenage McClenaghan in 2014 and together they rewrote the history books for Irish gymnastics.

McClenaghan won gold for Northern Ireland at the 2018 Commonwealth Games, and then won the first of his three European titles later that year - a feat he would also repeat in 2023 and 2024.

After a disappointing showing at the delayed Tokyo Olympics in 2021, the Newtownards gymnast bounced back to win back-to-back World Championships in 2022 and 2023.

The peak of their time together came the following year in Paris, when McClenaghan won Olympic gold with a superb routine in the final.

Carson added that their achievements together "once seemed impossible" and became a reality.

"Now that this chapter is coming to a close I can finally look back with an enormous sense of pride and recognise the magnitude of what was achieved and really against all odds.

"I'm incredibly grateful to everybody who supported me throughout this extraordinary journey."

Gymnastics Ireland confirmed to BBC Sport in a statement that Carson was no longer working with the sport's national body in Ireland, and it thanked him "for his hard work and dedication" in the role.

"We are incredibly proud of the achievements delivered through our working relationship with Luke over the past 10 years," Gymnastics Ireland said.

"The most notable of which being Rhys McClenaghan's historic gold in Paris 2024."

After his Olympics success, McClenaghan had surgery on a long-standing shoulder issue and only returned to action in February.

His first major tournament back was the Commonwealth Games in July, when he could only finish in sixth place in Glasgow, and he was seventh at the European Championship final the following month.

At the World Championships in October, without Carson in his corner, McClenaghan missed out on a place in the final as he struggled to regain the form that led him to Olympic gold.

Gymnastics Ireland said that Conor McGovern joined the men's national coaching team and will work alongside national coach Sergey Sizhanov in "guiding our men's programme towards LA 2028 and beyond, with a specific focus on working with Rhys".

Eamon Montgomery and Chester Enriquez have also been based out of Carson's Origin gym and will be impacted by the change.

"As we move forward, working in partnership with Sport Ireland & Sport Northern Ireland, we are excited about the new training program we have put in place in consultation with Rhys & our other LA 2028 potential gymnasts as we head into the Olympic qualification pathway next year," Gymnastics Ireland added.

articles.body: “I want to make it there too.”That was the thought that crossed Pooja Sahoo’s mind when fellow villager Sunelita Toppo broke into the Indian women’s hockey team as a teenager.Several years and countless training sessions later, the defender from Kukuda village in Odisha’s Sundargarh district has earned a maiden senior call-up of her own after being named in India’s squad for the Women’s Asian Champions Trophy, which begins in Bhopal on Thursday with the hosts taking on Malaysia in the opening match.For the 19-year-old, the selection is the culmination of a journey that began by watching players from the region and dreaming of following in their footsteps. “I started playing hockey when I was around 13 or 14 years old. There were many players around me and watching them play inspired me to take up the sport,” Pooja told TOI.Among those who inspired her was Sunelita, who had made the Indian team at the age of 16. “When she got her opportunity at such a young age, I felt that I wanted to reach that level too. My only goal was to make it to the senior team one day,” Pooja said.That ambition carried her through years in the junior setup. After progressing through Odisha’s hockey pathway, she trained at STC Centre in Sundargarh before moving to the National Centre of Excellence in New Delhi. She subsequently became a regular in the junior national programme, featuring on India’s Europe tour, playing in the Junior World Cup and helping the team win the Junior Women’s Asia Cup earlier this year.Pooja credits much of her growth to the experiences she gained in national camps and from learning under different coaches. One aspect of her game that has particularly impressed coaches is her drag-flicking ability. She first learnt the basics of drag-flicking under coach Pradeep Sarangi in Sundargarh before refining the skill during her time in Bengaluru and closely observing Harmanpreet Singh.The defender also believes her stint in the Hockey India League accelerated her development. Representing Shrachi Bengal Tigers, she had the opportunity to play alongside and learn from foreign stars, including Argentine drag-flick specialist Agustina Gorzelany. “It was a great experience playing with Gorzelany. She would often guide me and give me advice about different aspects of my game,” said Pooja.Known among her coaches for her vocal presence on the field, Pooja said communication came naturally to her. “I just enjoy expressing myself, sharing what I know and helping others. Communicating with teammates is something I enjoy,” she said.Now, with her first senior international tournament beckoning, Pooja is focussed on giving her absolute best. “I want to use everything I have learnt over the years and contribute as much as possible to the team’s success,” she added.She will get the chance to do exactly that on Thursday when Sjoerd Marijne-coached India open their campaign against Malaysia. Fresh from their Asian Games gold-medal triumph, the hosts will start as one of the favourites for the title, though Asian Games silver medallists China are expected to provide the sternest challenge despite the departure of coach Alyson Annan after more than four years in charge.Today’s matches: China vs Thailand, Japan vs South Korea, India vs Malaysia.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Peres Jepchirchir: World marathon champion gets three-year doping ban for using EPO
articles.summary: Reigning world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir is banned for three years for a doping violation.
articles.body:
Reigning world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been banned for three years for a doping violation.

The 33-year-old, who also won Olympic gold in 2021, was provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) in October after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for erythropoietin (EPO).

The sample was collected in Kenya prior to Jepchirchir winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026 and returned an adverse finding on 17 September.

She is one of three high-profile Kenyan athletes to have been sanctioned. Veronica Loleo has also been banned for three years after admitting using EPO, while Ronald Korir has received a six-year ban after failing to explain abnormalities found in his biological passport.

EPO is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.

If injected, it increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream but is only detectable in urine or blood for a short window of time.

Jepchirchir's other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.

While she denied using EPO, she signed an admission of violations form and accepted disqualification of all her competitive results since 17 July 2026.

"The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go," said Brett Clothier, chief executive of the AIU.

"The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.

"We will discuss the details behind these commitments with the Kenyan government in the coming months."

In September, Kenya was awarded the right to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships, with London and Rome missing out.

The decision increased scrutiny of the country's efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem, with more than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, having been suspended by the AIU since 2017.

Last month Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), told BBC Sport that Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility leading up to the 2029 event.

articles.title: Tres años de sanción por EPO para Peres Jepchirchir, campeona mundial de maratón
articles.standfirst: La keniana, oro olímpico en Tokio 2020, dio positivo en tres muestras de un control fuera de competición previo al Maratón de Sydney
articles.summary: La keniana, oro olímpico en Tokio 2020, dio positivo en tres muestras de un control fuera de competición previo al Maratón de Sydney
articles.body: Peres Jepchirchir estará tres años sancionada por dopaje. La Unidad para la Integridad del Atletismo (AIU) confirmó el miércoles el castigo a la vigente campeona mundial de maratón por su positivo por eritropoyetina (EPO) en un control fuera de competición. La keniana, oro olímpico en Tokio 2020, también ha ganado los maratones de Nueva York, Boston y Londres. El control se realizó el 17 de julio, antes de que Jepchirchir participara en el Maratón de Sydney. Según la AIU, ese día se recogieron dos muestras de sangre y cuatro de orina. Los análisis detectaron EPO en la primera muestra de sangre y en la primera y la cuarta de orina. Una vez notificado el positivo, la AIU entrevistó a Jepchirchir por videoconferencia el 20 de octubre. La atleta negó haber recibido una inyección o haberse administrado EPO y explicó que desconocía cómo había llegado la sustancia a su organismo. Siete días después, el 27 de octubre, la AIU recibió un escrito firmado por la atleta en el que admitía la infracción de la normativa antidopaje y aceptaba sus consecuencias. Esa admisión redujo de cuatro a tres años el periodo de sanción. Además, la vigente campeona del mundo de maratón ha sido vetada de por vida de los ocho 'majors', el circuito de los ocho mejores maratones del mundo. Jepchirchir, de 33 años y ganadora del oro olímpico en 2021, fue suspendida provisionalmente en octubre después que unos análisis desvelaran trazas de EPO en unas muestras tomadas antes del maratón de Sídney (Australia), celebrado en agosto pasado y que ganó con un crono de 2h18:31.

articles.title: La Federación Española repetirá el polémico sorteo de la Copa del Rey
articles.standfirst: Mientras intervenían los presentares y antes de abrirse las bolas, apareció en una pantalla un partido que luego se dio en la segunda ronda: el Eivissa - Cangas
articles.summary: Mientras intervenían los presentares y antes de abrirse las bolas, apareció en una pantalla un partido que luego se dio en la segunda ronda: el Eivissa - Cangas
articles.body: La Federación Española de Balonmano (RFEBM) comunicó a los clubes implicados que mañana, viernes, se volverá a realizar el sorteo de la segunda ronda de la Copa del Rey para evitar suspicacias tras lo sucedido este jueves. Mientras los presentadores anunciaban el nombre de los equipos que conformaban cada eliminatoria, en la pantalla apareció el emparejamiento entre el Handbol Club Eivissa y el Frigoríficos del Morrazo Cangas que posteriormente acabaría siendo el segundo enfrentamiento de esta ronda. Cabe reseñar que aún no se habían abierto bolas. La reclamación de la Federación Gallega de Balonmano provocó que el ente presidido por Francisco Blázquez decidiera anulara el resultado del sorteo y repetirlo mañana por la mañana. El Cangas había quedado emparejado con el Eivissa, el Cisne con el Proin BM Sevilla y el OAR Coruña con el Villa de Aranda. La propia RFEBM compartió en redes sociales la noticia de la repetición del sorteo y se ha explicado: "Por error apareció en pantalla el resultado de una prueba previa al mismo". Así fue el directo del sorteo en Youtube.

articles.title: Orissa HC questions Hockey India secretary general’s power to convene meetings
articles.summary: KOLKATA: The Orissa High Court has questioned whether Hockey India’s secretary general can convene Executive Board (EB) meetings without the orders or
articles.body: KOLKATA: The Orissa High Court has questioned whether Hockey India’s secretary general can convene Executive Board (EB) meetings without the orders or consent of federation president Dilip Kumar Tirkey, observing that the probable answer under its bye-laws is “not in the affirmative”.The observations came in the detailed order dismissing Hockey India’s plea to vacate the Nov 6 interim stay on its election process. The stay on the proposed elections continues, while the main writ petition remains pending. The order, passed on Wednesday, was made available on Thursday.Justice RK Pattanaik examined the authority under which Hockey India’s 119th and 120th EB meetings were convened. The 119th meeting, held in Tirkey’s absence, approved the proposal to conduct the elections and appoint an electoral officer. The 120th was convened by the secretary general and chaired by EB member Tapan Kumar Das.Examining Hockey India’s bye-laws, the court said no provision had been brought to its notice permitting the secretary general to convene meetings without the president’s orders or consent. It observed that the secretary general functions as the “Administrative Executor” of the president’s decision rather than as an independent convening authority.The court, however, stopped short of finally deciding the legality of the decisions taken at the meetings, saying the issue would be considered while disposing of the main writ petition. It clarified that its observations were confined to the interim applications.The court also noted that some other state units were in default but had not received notices similar to the one issued to the Hockey Association of Odisha (HAO), saying HAO’s apprehension of being singled out “may not be entirely misplaced”.It further observed that initiating the process to reclassify HAO from a permanent member to an associate member when Hockey India elections were proposed could give rise to an allegation of mala fide and had created a “trust deficit” between the parties.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: La denuncia de la italiana Sabbatini: "Sufrí acoso mientras corría, tenía miedo"
articles.standfirst: La atleta, oro europeo sub'23 de 1.500, ha asegurado que "unos hombres me siguieron cuando entrenaba. Tuve que cambiar de dirección"
articles.summary: La atleta, oro europeo sub'23 de 1.500, ha asegurado que "unos hombres me siguieron cuando entrenaba. Tuve que cambiar de dirección"
articles.body: No es la primera vez que una deportista denuncia los problemas de acoso que ha sufrido mientras entrenaba. La última ha sido la italiana Gaia Sabbatini, que ha asegurado que "me he visto seguida por gente en bicicleta en varias ocasiones; son experiencias traumáticas". En palabras que recoge 'Il Giornale', la campeona de Europa sub'23 de 1.500 asegura que "me ocurrió dos veces en Roma y una vez en Birmingham, en el canal. Unos hombres me siguieron. Me detuve y ellos también. Cambié de dirección, y ellos también. Era evidente que me seguían". Algunos estudios apuntan que un 68% de las corredoras (el 86% entre 18 y 24 años) han experimentado al menos un incidente de acoso durante su entrenamiento. "Antes era más relajada, ponía música y me movía con tranquilidad. Después de estas experiencias, ya no estoy tranquila. Ahora, por desgracia, me alarmo enseguida y tomo más precauciones: si veo a alguien detrás de mí, lo observo durante más tiempo, hago pruebas exhaustivas", continuó explicando la atleta. La italiana pidió más educación para contrarrestar esos casos de acoso. "Todo comienza en la infancia. La educación sexual y emocional debe impartirse en las escuelas, porque estas personas con problemas no comprenden que asustan a otros con ciertos comportamientos; otras son violentas con las mujeres, como lo demuestran las noticias", afirmó. Pero Sabbatini aboga por seguir saliendo a correr al aire libre y no encerrarse con una cinta. "Sería una locura. He oído comentarios sexistas en la calle. Los ignoro, pero lo que más me preocupa es el miedo. Nunca camino sola; lo evito. Tengo la ubicación de mi hermana en mi teléfono". Recientemente la atleta Laura Rodríguez denunció en sus redes sociales haber sido víctima de una agresión sexual mientras se entrenaba. En un mensaje en el que explicaba que se tuvo que retirar de la Carrera 'Bimbo Global Race', la deportista, que fue madre hace un año, explicó que "alzo la voz porque el pasado 12 septiembre sufrí una agresión sexual mientras entrenaba a plena luz del día. Ninguna mujer tendríamos que pasar por esto. Alzo la voz porque yo sólo estaba entrenando". Antes que ella fue Carla García la que hizo público que sufrió un episodio de acoso mientras realizaba series en un parque del sur de Madrid. La vallista, campeona de España sub 23 de 400 metros vallas, aseguró que un hombre, de unos 50 años, se escondió detrás de una valla para hacerle fotografías en el momento en el que estaba entrenando junto a su técnico. "He oído varios clics que provenían de detrás de una valla. Me he dado cuenta de que había un móvil que rápidamente ha desaparecido", dijo. También en Portugal la marchadora olímpica portuguesa Ines Henriques, denunció en 2022 el acoso de un desconocido, que le enseñó sus genitales mientras ella entrenaba en la localidad de Rio Maior, en el centro de Portugal. Esta inseguridad que sienten las mujeres en los espacios para la práctica deportiva, acreditado en España en encuestas en las que el 93% de las entrevistadas reconocía haber sentido miedo al hacer deporte al aire libre, llevó a la Asociación para Mujeres en el Deporte Profesional (AMDP), en colaboración con Uriaxait, a desarrollar 'Entrena Segura', una WebAPP basada en inteligencia artificial que recoge, analiza y transforma en datos e información las sensaciones de inseguridad o miedo que viven las mujeres en las instalaciones deportivas.

articles.title: “I didn’t want my son to be out here alone”: Anthony Joshua opens up about how thoughts of his own death led him to welcome a daughter with ex Nicole Osbourne
articles.summary: Anthony Joshua, the popular British boxer and 2012 Olympic super heavyweight gold medalist, has mostly preferred to keep his personal life out of the
articles.body: Anthony Joshua, the popular British boxer and 2012 Olympic super heavyweight gold medalist, has mostly preferred to keep his personal life out of the spotlight even though he has recently announced the birth of his baby girl. While he has not been able to meet his newborn yet due to his professional commitments, he has opened up about the reason why he and his ex girlfriend, Nicole Osbourne decided to have one more child.Anthony Joshua reflects why he wanted to father one more child for his son, JJ, along with his ex girlfriend Nicole OsbourneA few days ago, in an interview with The Sun, the Olympic champion Anthony Joshua said, “This past year has been incredibly tough, I realised how precious life is, and how short it can be. I’m just going to live my life by duty, and even having a baby girl was part of my duty. I wanted to bring life in, it was a conscious decision, 100 per cent. If something happened to me, I didn’t want JJ to be out here alone.”Anthony Joshua also reflected on how he wants to launch more initiatives to help women around him as he added, “I love working alongside single mothers, working with charities that work with single parents, because women are amazing and they carry so much.”The 2012 Olympic super heavyweight gold medalist added, “So now I’ve got a daughter, maybe me and her can set something up where we’re doing things with women, and just showing that feminine side of me. I want to bring women together, honour women, catering for them, you know?”Anthony Joshua’s car crash which changed his perspective on lifeFor the unversed, Anthony Joshua went through a pretty challenging time after he found himself involved in a brutal car crash which happened last year.British boxer Anthony Joshua survived a fatal car crash on December 29, 2025, on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway in Ogun State, Nigeria, which killed two members of his team, Sina Ghami and Latif Ayodele.The Olympic champion Anthony Joshua was riding in the back of a Lexus SUV when the driver allegedly lost control while overtaking and collided with a stationary lorry.Later, driver Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode was charged in Ogun State with offenses including causing death by dangerous driving and driving without a valid license, and he has denied the charges. Stationary lorry driver Abubakar Adamu was also charged with obstructing traffic and denied the charge. Kayode's trial hearing was adjourned to November 17, 2026.Though Anthony Joshua survived the car crash, he ended up losing two people who stood by him through the beginning of his career.With the birth of his daughter, it seems Anthony Joshua has found happiness in his life again after a traumatic few months.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: La nueva vida de Duane da Rocha: de la piscina olímpica a azafata de Iberia
articles.standfirst: La campeona europea de los 200 metros espalda, que de pequeña soñaba con ser piloto, cuenta a MARCA cómo es su vida tras la retirada y su nueva etapa profesional
articles.summary: La campeona europea de los 200 metros espalda, que de pequeña soñaba con ser piloto, cuenta a MARCA cómo es su vida tras la retirada y su nueva etapa profesional
articles.body: A Duane da Rocha siempre le ha gustado volar. "Antes de irme al Centro de Alto Rendimiento de Madrid con 16 años quería ser piloto", confiesa a MARCA. "Un compañero de clase quería serlo y me pareció una fantasía de profesión", recuerda entre risas. Se lo dijo a sus padres y ellos estudiaron cómo hacer realidad el sueño de su hija. Barajaron la idea de que estudiase en un instituto militar para sacarse la licencia, pero ya estaba en el mundo de la natación y acabó pesando más el sueño de ir a unos Juegos Olímpicos. Al final lo hizo realidad dos veces: Londres 2012 y Río 2016. La campeona europea de los 200 metros espalda (Berlín 2014) y bronce mundial en la misma distancia en piscina corta (Estambul 2012) tenía en sus planes seguir hasta los Juegos de Tokio 2020. Pero quería prepararlos en su tierra, en Málaga y con su entrenador. Para ello necesitaba un club que le apoyase en el camino. Venía de una época de "bajón de resultados", como ella misma dice, y no lo encontró en Andalucía sino en el País Vasco, pero económicamente no le permitía dedicarse al cien por cien a la natación. "Físicamente me veía capaz de llegar a Tokio, pero estaba muy cansada emocionalmente. Estaba vacía. Y al final colgué el bañador porque ya no me merecía la pena", confiesa. Tenía casi 31 años. "Valoré las opciones. Era el momento de buscarme la vida de verdad y no de seguir luchando por un sueño que tenía fecha de caducidad", añade. Y anunció su retirada en 2019. No había preparado lo que vendría después del deporte porque, reconoce, su adiós fue casi de un día para otro. "Lo que sabía seguro es que después de 20 años dedicándome a la natación, que era algo que me apasionaba, me daba pánico acabar en un trabajo que no me gustase. Después de una vida llena de rutinas, quería un cambio drástico. Algo que fuera diferente cada día", explica. Una amiga, que también había sido nadadora, le contó su nueva vida como azafata y sembró de nuevo en Duane la semillita de volar, aunque ya no como piloto. Si cogen un vuelo de Iberia hoy en día, quizá se la encuentren entre la tripulación de cabina. De hecho, más de una vez algún pasajero la ha reconocido. "Y me ha dado una vergüenza...", reconoce entre risas. No ha coincidido en vuelos con ex compañeras o rivales, pero sí con waterpolistas, algún director técnico de la RFEN, fisioterapeutas y con Fred Vergnoux, el que fuera entrenador de Mireia Belmonte. "Como es inesperado, se sorprenden", reconoce. Tras pasar por varias compañías aéreas, recaló en Iberia en marzo de 2024. "Estoy súper feliz porque cada mes es diferente. En la natación siempre éramos los mismos", dice. A sus 38 años, Da Rocha está encantada porque hace vuelos transoceánicos a América. "Estoy desbloqueando destinos, el que me apasiona es Miami", confiesa. El próximo vuelo en su agenda es Costa Rica. El 16-17 de este mes le darán los destinos de diciembre. Cada mes hace varios vuelos a cuatro o cinco rutas distintas. Durante su etapa como nadadora de élite viajó mucho pero no le daba tiempo a ver nada más allá de la piscina de competición, el hotel y sus alrededores. Hoy en día trata de encontrar tiempo en los diferentes destinos para poder conocerlos. Lo que no suele hacer es nadar en las piscinas de los hoteles. "A mí me encanta nadar para competir y si no, me aburro. Necesito un objetivo para que me llene", explica. De hecho, reconoce que estuvo tentada a volver para los Juegos de París 2024. En un parón de trabajo entre una compañía aérea y otra, ejerció como monitora en el Club Natación Mijas y al enseñar a los niños, éstos le contagiaron su pasión y le devolvieron el gusanillo por la competición. Empezó a entrenar para ayudar al club. Fue a la Copa de Andalucía, la Copa de España, se metió en una final... "Volví a sentir la emoción de conseguir resultados. Me vine arriba y empecé a obsesionarme otra vez y a pensar en París. Pero volví a poner los pies en el suelo y abandoné la idea", desvela. Echando la vista atrás, se queda con los aprendizajes de su etapa como nadadora. "Fue una vida alucinante que me hizo muy feliz, pero también aprendí mucho de momentos no tan buenos que me hicieron crecer como persona. El deporte de élite es un ambiente hostil, te enfrentas a esa hostilidad desde muy joven y creces a pasos agigantados. Enfrentarme luego al mundo real fue duro porque sales de una burbuja, pero el deporte me enseñó a relativizar y no obcecarme cuando las cosas no salen bien. Cuando pasa eso, hay que analizarlo para que no se vuelva a repetir, pero siempre mirando hacia adelante", reflexiona. A día de hoy, lo único que echa de menos de la natación es "competir y sentirme fuerte. Esa sensación de empoderamiento no se consigue con ninguna otra cosa que no sea la competición de élite. Lo que no echo de menos es el proceso que hay que pasar para sentirte así".

articles.body:
It's Philadelphia Marathon Weekend, and the fun in Philly has already begun. The weekend's festivities kicked off on Friday with the Philadelphia Marathon Weekend Expo. The expo will resume on Saturday, though many fans will turn their attention to the road.

The Philadelphia Half-Marathon will take place on Saturday, along with the 8K. The Philadelphia Kids Run and Philadelphia Marathon will take place on Sunday.

It's going to be a wonderful weekend for race and fitness fans along one of the nation's most iconic settings. The course will begin and end along Benjamin Franklin Parkway, near the Philadelphia Museum of Art—you know, the one Sylvester Stallone carried into film history.

Time: 6:55 a.m. ET (push-rim wheelchairs); 7 a.m. (runners and walkers)

Location: 22nd St. & Benjamin Franklin Pkwy.

The Philadelphia Marathon isn't as large as, say, the New York City Marathon, which recorded over 60,000 finishers this year. However, it has grown exponentially since its first iteration began in 1994.

"Each year, the City of Philadelphia and Philadelphia Marathon Weekend set out to create a race weekend that is a memorable experience for both runners and spectators," said David G. Wilson, Executive Director for Philadelphia Marathon Weekend, per the event's official website .

This year, 20,000 participants have registered for the full marathon, with another 15,000 registering for the half-marathon. While that falls short of some of the biggest marathons in the country, it's still going to be a massive event in one of the nation's most historic cities.

"There's the city itself," wrote Kristen Schott of PhillyMag.com. "The businesses come alive for the fun."

Speaking of history, it's worth noting that the men's and women's course records were both set in 2021. Mike Chesire claimed the men's record with a time of 2:13:28, while Leslie Sexton claimed the women's record with a time of 2:28:24. Kassian Eaton set the non-binary record in 2023 with a time of 2:35:38.

Melikhaya Frans and Anna Oeser won the men's and women's races, respectively, last year, while Bryce Ott won the non-binary division. Miguel Vergara won the men's wheelchair division, while Hannah Babalola won the women's wheelchair.

This year's race will feature a record crowd and an expanded weekend expo but will take a familiar course that begins and ends near the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

articles.title: Why some love stories are worth their weight in gold
articles.summary: Simran Sharma was born extremely pre-term — at six-and-a-half months — grossly underweight and feeble. Doctors said her chances of survival were slim.
articles.body: Simran Sharma was born extremely pre-term — at six-and-a-half months — grossly underweight and feeble. Doctors said her chances of survival were slim. Relatives said, “It’s okay, it’s only a girl,” she was told later. But the baby lived, somehow.That early trait of beating crushing odds is a recurring and defining feature of Simran’s life. Last month, the 27-year-old sprinted to a rare golden double (with her guide runner Shivam) in 100m and 200m at Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.Para-athletes are classified according to levels of impairment. Her category, T12, is for athletes whose vision is limited to a radius of less than 5 degrees. “Nothing”, she says, “has come easily to me in life.”Childhood was hard for Simran, who was born in Modinagar, about 50km north-east of Delhi. Her father was bedbound for years. Her mother cooked and cleaned hostels to put food on the table. “She would make sanitary pads and take a train to Delhi to sell them,” the para-athlete recalls. Yet, affection was abundant at home. “Maybe because parents shower more attention on the weaker child,” she says.Simran realised early she had speed. “In Class VI, I ran in a salwar-suit in a village sports meet and won a bunch of medals,” she remembers. But when she started training with a couple of other girls at the local MM College ground, social roadblocks emerged. Relatives and neighbours warned her family that practising with boys might lead the young girl astray. But her parents refused to back down. “They supported me all along,” Simran says, with gratitude and pride.Two incidents further steeled her. In Class X, a teacher slapped Simran in front of other students, mistaking her for another girl. “I felt she hit me because I had failed to win a medal. I practised hard and won a clutch of medals the next time.” Also embossed in her memory is the sight of her mother crying and pleading before the principal, who had once refused to send her for an inter-school meet.Till 18, Simran ran in open events. Due to her restrictive visual condition, she would occasionally stray into a neighbouring lane, leading to small fights. But she kept winning races.Yet, early success couldn’t spur her to dream big. “Poor kids often lack confidence. I just wanted to win at the state level. I hoped to become a physical instructor at school. Sapne seemit thhey (My dreams were limited),” she says.In 2015, she met Gajendra Singh, an Army serviceman from Khanjarpur, a village 3km from Modinagar. He would train in the same ground, sometimes dragging a tyre behind. “We would laugh. But he would offer help, motivate us,” she says. Slowly, they became friends.“We spoke on the phone, exchanged messages. Sau messages milte tthey (I would get a 100 messages),” she laughs. They got married in 2017.Gajendra was confident of her shining on bigger platforms. He sold a 100-yard plot of family land in Modinagar, invested in her special diet, shoes and sportswear. But the timings didn’t improve. “One day Gajju asked my coach, ‘Why isn’t she progressing?’ He replied in anger, ‘If you can make her run faster, go ahead.’ Gajju felt bad. He took it up as a challenge,” feels Simran.The jawan would take two months’ leave, read up articles on sprint, take online courses and create a training regimen that was “insane”. “Sometimes, I felt like fainting. I would hide. I would lie, pretend I had a headache. He would prepare a diet chart. I would throw it away. But he would just say, ‘You think I am your enemy now. But the day you win the medal, you will love me the most’,” laughs Simran, who idolises Cuban sprint legend Omara Durand.2019 was a dark year. “My father, who passed away in 2020, was on a ventilator. I was injured. My husband was in debt. He would be taunted for wasting his time on me. I was under extreme stress. I wrote a letter in blood saying sorry because I wasn’t able to do anything for him,” she confesses.But Gajendra hauled her back from the abyss. “He told me, ‘Girta kaun nahi hai. Tum girogi main tumhe uthaunga. Tum phir girogi, main phir uthaunga. Par main tumhe haarne nahi doonga (Everyone falls down. Every time you fall, I will lift you. I will not let you lose)’,” she says.The tide began to turn when she became part of Olympic Gold Quest, an NGO that supports athletes, in 2020. Simran became aware of the science of sports: nutrition supplements, rehabilitation, strength conditioning, and the works. “Their support was life-changing,” she acknowledges.The breakthrough came in 2022. Simran won two silvers in Hangzhou Asian Para Games. The priceless medals also fetched Rs 3 crore. “I gifted my mom a home, bought land for my family,” says Simran, relaxing at her new Krishna Kunj residence on the outskirts of Modinagar.She also treasures the 200m bronze (guide runner Abhay Singh) from the 2024 Paris Paralympic. “My mother kept praying in a temple after I had finished fourth in my favourite 100m,” says the athlete, also a 200m gold medalist in World Championships. “A gold in 2028 LA is our next target,” says Simran, who lives and trains in Delhi’s Jawaharlal Nehru sports stadium.“People see the glitter of medals. They don’t know the struggle behind them. In every athlete’s story, you only see the medallist. In our story, you can see both Gajju and me,” says Simran, who coincidentally shares her name with the female protagonist of ‘Dilwale Dulhaniya Le Jayenge’.Theirs, too, is a special love story.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Gagan Narang emerges frontrunner for IOA president’s post
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: With the nomination process for the Indian Olympic Association's (IOA) 2026-2030 elections beginning on Sunday, the race for key positions in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: With the nomination process for the Indian Olympic Association's (IOA) 2026-2030 elections beginning on Sunday, the race for key positions in the country's premier sports body has gathered momentum, with Gagan Narang emerging as a likely consensus candidate for the president's post from the govt side, sources tracking developments told TOI.Narang, the incumbent vice-president and an Olympic medallist, has made a strong pitch for himself in recent days, holding meetings with influential people in political circles as the govt looks to shape the IOA leadership for the next four years. Sources indicated that Narang is almost certain to file his nomination and has emerged as the preferred candidate.The incumbent president P T Usha, who has found her way back into the electoral race after securing nomination as the female representative from the Ice Hockey Association of India (IHAI), is likely to contest against Narang, her camp has indicated.However, the National Sports Federations (NSFs), which account for 60 votes in the electoral college, are still weighing their options. While a section is believed to be considering backing a govt-supported candidate, others are exploring the possibility of rallying behind Usha to trump Narang or fielding their own candidate to avoid splitting votes.Former Athletics Federation of India (AFI) chief Adille Sumariwalla, former IOA secretary general Rajeev Mehta and former Delhi state BJP president and Archery Association of India (AAI) secretary general Virender Sachdeva are among the names being discussed.Sachdeva has emerged as a possible dark horse in the presidential race. With his political connections and longstanding association with sports administration, he is believed to enjoy acceptability among both political circles and several NSFs, making him a potential consensus choice if the race takes an unexpected turn, sources said.The elections also assume significance with Ahmedabad set to host the 2030 CWG and India's ambitious Olympic bid for 2036 gaining traction. Gujarat-based administrators Chintan Parikh, Ajay H Patel and Udit Sheth are likely to secure key positions in the incoming executive council (EC), as TOI has previously reported.The nomination process will run until Nov 24, after which returning officer Sanjay K Srivastava is expected to finalise the candidates.Meanwhile, it's been learnt the Boxing Federation of India (BFI) has failed to secure voting rights. The federation, embroiled in internal disputes and recognition issues, was excluded from the electoral college for IOA polls. The Delhi High Court had referred BFI's plea for voting rights to the returning officer for a hearing. However, sources said the federation was not granted relief.The Indian Golf Union's (IGU) rival factions have also approached Srivastava following the high court's directive for a hearing on Monday. The Table Tennis Federation of India, meanwhile, is unlikely to get relief as its suspension-related matter remains before the court. The two federations were also excluded from the electoral college because of their internal disputes.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: Protección Civil de la Generalitat mantiene activada la alerta por fuertes vientos
articles.body: La caída de un árbol en la avenida de la Meridiana de Barcelona al paso de las participantes en la Cursa de les Dones este domingo en la capital catalana ha dejado a varias mujeres heridas, que están siendo atendidas por los sanitarios del Sistema de Emergencias Médicas. Protección Civil de la Generalitat mantiene activada este domingo la alerta por fuertes vientos, que pueden superar los 72 kilómetros por hora en puntos del litoral y prelitoral central y sur, mientras que el Ayuntamiento de Barcelona activó la pasada noche su propio plan municipal de prevención. La 22 ª Cursa de les Dones de Barcelona ha partido con la participación de miles de mujeres a las nueve de la mañana desde la confluencia de Bac de Roda con la calle de Huelva, en el distrito de Sant Martí, y debía finalizar en las inmediaciones del Parc de la Ciutadella.

articles.title: Kwizera da una exhibición en el cross de Atapuerca, en el que Cherop gana al esprint
articles.standfirst: Rodrigue superó al etíope Aregawi para llevarse la victoria en una carrera clave para el equipo del próximo Europeo y en la que ADA Calvià - Vistasol y Bilbao Atletismo ganaron por clubes
articles.summary: Rodrigue superó al etíope Aregawi para llevarse la victoria en una carrera clave para el equipo del próximo Europeo y en la que ADA Calvià - Vistasol y Bilbao Atletismo ganaron por clubes
articles.body: Rodrigue Kwizera dio una exhibición en el circuito arqueológico del cross de Atapuerca para adjudicarse una impresionante victoria ante el etíope Aregawi, subcampeón olímpico de 10.000 metros, en categoría masculina, mientras que en féminas se impuso la keniata Mirriam Cherop al esprint en la recta final. Por segundo año consecutivo este cross burgalés coincidió con el Nacional de campo a través por clubes. Además, la cita repartía plazas para el Europeo de la especialidad, que se disputará el 13 de diciembre en Belgrado, ya que los cuatro primeros atletas elegibles en categoría absoluta estarán en la competición continental. Sin duda, uno de los grandes nombres propios de la jornada fue el de Rodrigue Kwizera, que respondió con rotundidad a los primeros ataques solventes de Aregawi, encargado de romper la carrera tras 15 minutos de prueba e incipientes cambios de ritmo de Dani Arce, primero, e Ilias Fifa, después. Así, Aregawi, Kwizera y el keniata Kiboino se situaron en cabeza, pero el pulso iban a mantenerlo hasta el final el etíope y el español. En esa pugna, Kwizera, que aún no puede competir como internacional con España al no tener el 'tránsfer' de World Athletics, dejó atrás a su rival con un soberbio ataque, que le permitió festejar la victoria en los metros finales, antes de cruzar la meta en 22:38 y reeditar su último triunfo de 2024. Al atleta de Playas de Castellón le acompañaron en el podio Aregawi (22:41) y Ayele (22:45). El primer español fue Miguel Ángel Chazarra, séptimo con 23:04, por delante de Oukhelfen, octavo, con 23:12. En la prueba femenina, las africanas se situaron en cabeza tras los primeros kilómetros, con Nadia Battocletti, que defendía la victoria de la pasada edición, como única 'invitada' europea entre ellas. Pero la subcampeona olímpica de 10.000 metros, que llegaba de una lesión que le impidió estar en Itálica, cedió antes de la última vuelta. La etíope Asefa, que había liderado la carrera en varios momentos, se vio superada en la recta final por la keniata Mirriam Cherop, que remontó para llevarse la victoria al esprint (25:56), por delante de las etíopes Asefa y Asefu Abreha, que completaron el podio con el mismo tiempo. Battocletti cruzó quinta la meta (26:09), mientras que Carla Gallardo fue la primera española, novena (26:38), por delante de Idaira Prieto. ADA Calvià - Vistasol y Bilbao Atletismo hicieron historia en este Nacional de cross por clubes, que coincidía por segundo año consecutivo con la rueba de Atapuerca. Con Mathew Kipchumba Kipsang al frente, el ADA Calvià - Vistasol logró su primer título en esta competición, con 28 puntos, por delante del Playas de Castellón (41) y Vicky Foods Athletics (59). Por su parte, Bilbao Atletismo, con Idaira Prieto y Carolina Robles entre ellas, sumaron su undécimo título nacional de cross (19 puntos), el club más laureado de la historia en categoría masculina o femenina, por delante de Vicky Foods Athletics (36) y Cárnicas Serrano (38).

articles.title: Chanchal Surjit Singh rues lack of recognition for India's 1974 Women's Hockey World Cup team
articles.summary: KOLKATA: Fifty-two years is a long time, but for Chanchal Surjit Singh, a member of the Indian women’s team at the 1974 World Cup, the memories remain
articles.body: KOLKATA: Fifty-two years is a long time, but for Chanchal Surjit Singh, a member of the Indian women’s team at the 1974 World Cup, the memories remain vivid.India finished fourth in their maiden World Cup hockey campaign in Mandelieu, France, an achievement Chanchal believes has never received the recognition it deserved. Now, watching another generation make its mark, she is delighted.The current team finished fifth at this year’s World Cup, India’s best result since 1974, before winning Asian Games gold for the first time in 44 years.“India’s women team played their first World Cup and finished fourth, but there’s is hardly any recognition,” said Chanchal, who also led the team during a Test series and was awarded the Maharaja Ranjit Singh award.The lack of acknowledgement is particularly striking for Chanchal when compared to the tributes accorded to India’s 1975 men’s World Cup triumph, in which her husband Surjit Singh was an important member of the team.“The 1975 team gets a lot of accolades, and that makes me very happy because my husband was also part of that team,” she said.For Chanchal, however, playing in the World Cup remains the defining achievement of her career. “If I look at my sporting career, playing in the 1974 World Cup was the biggest moment. Even today, it inspires me because I feel I achieved something in life.”Much has changed since her playing days from 1968 to 1975, when players had few of the facilities now taken for granted. “We would eat at home and go to play. If there was an India camp, maybe we would get some additional diet there. That was about it,” she recalled during an interaction at her home in Mohali.Chanchal is therefore pleased with the support available to today’s players, from better diet and equipment to scholarships, specialised coaching and modern training facilities.“I am very happy that players are being looked after now. If you want to compete with the rest of the world, you have to support them in every possible way. They need good coaching and proper facilities.”An avid follower of the sport, Chanchal watched India’s World Cup matches and was impressed by the current side’s speed and combination. “Their speed was very good, the combination was good and they were passing the ball very well. It was a very quick game,” she said.For someone from a generation when opportunities for women were limited, the progress carries particular meaning.“At that time, we could not even think about opportunities like the ones players have today. Sometimes I imagine that if these opportunities had existed in our time, perhaps we too could have achieved more,” she said.“But I am very happy that the generations coming after us are doing so well and that the government and parents are supporting them.”Her association with sport continued after her playing career. Chanchal spent around 26 years with the Punjab Sports Department, joining as an assistant director and eventually rising to joint director.Having witnessed Indian women’s hockey evolve from 1974 to the successes of the present generation, she believes bigger milestones can follow. “Indian hockey went down for some time, but now it is progressing again. I believe that, going forward, we will win medals at the Olympics and hopefully win the World Cup too.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Red Wings trade Dylan Larkin to Canadiens in NHL blockbuster
articles.summary: Dylan Larkin finally has his landing spot.
articles.body:
Dylan Larkin finally has his landing spot.

The Red Wings are trading their ex-captain to the Canadiens for three players and four future draft picks, the team announced on Sunday.

Forward Kirby Dach, goaltender Samuel Montembeault and the rights to forward Michael Hage are heading to Detroit along with conditional first-round picks in 2027 and 2029, a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fourth-rounder.

Detroit is also sending its 2028 second-round pick and 2027 third-rounder.

The trade is a long time coming after Larkin very publicly requested a trade ahead of the season. He was stripped of his captaincy and has forfeited over $1 million after being suspended without pay on Oct. 29.

Larkin, who won a gold medal with Team USA at the 2026 Olympics, reportedly cited the Red Wings' 10-year playoff drought as a major reason for requesting the trade.

It's the latest blockbuster deal in a stretch that's been full of them for the American Olympic roster. Connor Hellebuyck was suspended to begin the season before the Jets traded him to the Devils last month. Brady Tkachuk requested a trade from the Senators and was dealt to the Panthers before the season started.

Reigning MVP Nikita Kucherov has also requested a trade, though he remains playing on the Lightning's top line and it's unclear if a deal is coming.

articles.title: El youtuber IShowSpeed acelera más que Usain Bolt y corre los 100 metros en 10,35: "Iré a los Juegos Olímpicos"
