articles.summary: IShowSpeed lleva más de un año entrenando con Ato Boldon y ha impresionado a Usain Bolt por su aceleración y velocidad
articles.body: El streamer, youtuber y creador de contenido estadounidense IShowSpeed (21 años) registra unos impresionantes 10,352 segundos en los 100 metros, dejando a Usain Bolt impresionado. En el episodio titulado 'Corrí contra Usain Bolt' (I races Usain Bolt!), el segundo de la temporada Speed Goes Pro, el streamer que llevaba meses entrenándose logró correr los 100 metros lisos en 10,352 segundos en su segundo intento. Eso sí, con un pequeño asterisco ya que Speed contó con una pequeña ventaja al salir desde los tacos unos metros antes del incio de los 100 metros. Los récords de España absolutos de los 100 metros lisos reconocidos por la Real Federación Española de Atletismo (RFEA) son 10,06 segundos en categoría masculina y 11,06 segundos en categoría femenina. El récord mundial de los 100 metros lisos femenino es de 10,49 segundos, logrado por la atleta estadounidense Florence Griffith-Joyner el 16 de julio de 1988. Ato Boldon, cuatro veces medallista olímpico, ha entrenado a Speed desde septiembre de 2025 y ha elogiado su compromiso: "Pensé que duraría dos semanas, pero la verdad es que vino a entrenar, siguió viniendo, llega puntual y se esfuerza mucho... Llevamos ya más de un año trabajando juntos; su cuerpo está empezando a cambiar y ya tiene el aspecto adecuado". Aunque no es un tiempo oficial de competición y queda a 0,772 segundos del récord mundial de Bolt (9,58), las gráficas mostraron que su aceleración en los primeros 15 metros superó la velocidad inicial del jamaicano. El ocho veces campeón olímpico se mostró sorprendido por la velocidad alcanzada por IShowSpeed, un youtuber sin pasado en el atletismo. Usain Bolt, que le ofreció varios consejos a IShowSpeed, cree que el famoso streamer tiene potencial para convertirse en velocista profesional. "Creo que sí", dijo Bolt cuando Speed le preguntó si podría convertirse en profesional. Speed dejó claro su objetivo: "En 2028, sin duda, estaré compitiendo en los Juegos Olímpicos".

articles.title: Rajeev Mehta files nomination for IOA president's post; Yogeshwar Dutt for Executive Council member
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Fencing Association of India (FAI) secretary Rajeev Mehta on Monday filed his nomination for the post of Indian Olympic Association (IOA)
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Fencing Association of India (FAI) secretary Rajeev Mehta on Monday filed his nomination for the post of Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president. It was the second day of the nomination process, with no candidature filed on the opening day. Tuesday is the final day for nominations, with Archery Association of India (AAI) secretary general Virender Sachdeva, current IOA vice-president Gagan Narang and incumbent president PT Usha among those expected to enter the race.Besides Mehta, Swimming Federation of India (SFI) president RN Jayaprakash, Indian Kayaking & Canoeing Association's Prashant Kushwaha and former wrestler Yogeshwar Dutt have filed their nominations for Executive Council member posts. Dutt, a London 2012 bronze medallist, is among four male athletes to have come through the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOMs) route.The nominations were filed as part of a coordinated exercise at the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) office in the capital on Monday afternoon. The process covered the posts of IOA president, senior vice-president, vice-presidents (male and female), treasurer, joint secretaries (male and female) and Executive Council members, with candidates finalising their proposers and seconders.IOA treasurer Sahdev Yadav, Maninder Pal Singh (Cycling Federation of India), Rajeev Mehta, Rani Rampal (female SOMs), Dutt (SOMs), Amitabh Sharma (Ice Skating Association of India), Bhupender Singh Bajwa (Wushu Association of India), Kamlesh Mehta (male SOMs), Nitin Gupta (Indian Triathlon Federation), Mukesh Kumar (Judo Federation of India), Balaji Maradapa (Rowing Federation of India) and Sunaina Kumari (Bowling Federation of India) were among those present.TimesofIndia.com has reliably learnt that Virender Sachdeva has emerged as a strong contender for the IOA president's post. His political connections and longstanding association with Indian sport in an administrative capacity have strengthened his position among national sports federations (NSFs) and in government circles.Sunaina Kumari, daughter of late veteran sports administrator and former Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) president Raja Randhir Singh, has emerged as a contender for the women's vice-president post.The nominations list is expected to be announced on Tuesday evening. articles.title: Verdeliss: "Cuando fui capaz de gestionar el miedo, empecé a confiar otra vez en mi cuerpo"
articles.standfirst: El documental de Movistar Plus 'Verdeliss. Más allá del miedo' repasa la preparación de Estefanía Unzu para el Mundial de 100 km, sus entrenamientos y sus dudas ante esa gran cita
articles.summary: El documental de Movistar Plus 'Verdeliss. Más allá del miedo' repasa la preparación de Estefanía Unzu para el Mundial de 100 km, sus entrenamientos y sus dudas ante esa gran cita
articles.body: Se mueve por retos, desde correr 12 maratones en 12 meses a completar siete maratones en siete continentes en 7 días. Sin embargo, uno de los últimos grandes desafíos de Estefanía Unzu, más conocida en redes sociales como 'Verdeliss', ha sido el Mundial de 100 kilómetros, que disputó en septiembre con el equipo español en su primera internacionalidad. En la presentación de 'Verdeliss. Más allá del miedo', una miniserie documental de dos capítulos que ha estrenado este lunes Movistar Plus, la ultrafondista repasa cómo fue la preparación de esta gran cita, en la que ganó la plata junto al equipo, acabó sexta en categoría absoluta y fue primera de su grupo de edad. Así, durante las semanas previas a la cita mundialistas, las cámaras siguieron a 'Verdeliss' en sus entrenamientos, rutinas familiares y momentos de máxima tensión competitiva, retratando la dureza del ultrafondo y el desgaste físico extremo y el mental, que le hizo incluso pensar en renunciar. "Mi percepción era que había dejado de tener buenas sensaciones", aseguró Estefanía Unzu en la presentación del documental, una producción original de TBS (productora creativa de Telefónica). "Mis padres me decían que era el subconsciente, pero yo no lo veía. Después me hice pruebas físicas y el médico que me lleva viendo años me dijo que estaba mejor que nunca. Cuando fui capaz de gestionar la angustia, la ansiedad y el miedo, empecé a confiar en mi cuerpo y podía correr, ahí salieron las cosas". Empresaria y madre de ocho hijos, la atleta explicó que "te tienes que currar los objetivos y en los momentos decisivos hay que pensar que pones en bandeja todo el esfuerzo, el sacrificio, la disciplina... Mi familia me ha enseñado que no estaba sola en esto. Ellos fueron los que me 'sacaron' de casa en los momentos difíciles".

articles.title: Ndikumwenayo lidera a España para los Europeos de cross con la incógnita de Kwizera
articles.standfirst: Rodrigue Kwizera, actual plusmarquista nacional de 10 km ruta y media maratón, está pendiente de un transfer de World Athletic para participar en competiciones internacionales
articles.summary: Rodrigue Kwizera, actual plusmarquista nacional de 10 km ruta y media maratón, está pendiente de un transfer de World Athletic para participar en competiciones internacionales
articles.body: Thierry Ndikumwenayo, vigente campeón de Europa individual, lidera al equipo español que participará en los Europeos de cross de Belgrado (Serbia) del 13 de diciembre, en los que podría estar Rodrigue Kwizera, actual plusmarquista nacional de 10km ruta y media maratón y que está pendiente de un transfer de World Athletics con la autorización para participar en competiciones internacionales. El equipo absoluto masculino viaja a Belgrado con el objetivo de defender los títulos europeos por equipos conquistados en Antalya (Turquía) en 2024 y Lagoa (Portugal) en 2025. La preselección la encabeza Thierry Ndikumwenayo, que regresará a la competición internacional después de perderse por lesión el Campeonato de Europa de Birmingham 2026. Su última participación con la selección fue en el Mundial de Campo a Través de Tallahassee en enero, donde firmó una histórica octava posición y fue el mejor europeo de la prueba. Junto a él, Rodrigue Kwizera, de origen burundés, podría debutar con España. Su presencia está condicionada a recibir a tiempo el transfer de World Athletics con la autorización para representar a España en las competiciones internacionales. Junto a él figura el olímpico Abdessamad Oukhelfen, uno de los pilares del equipo que conquistó el oro en Lagoa gracias a su sexta posición individual y que afronta su séptimo Europeo después de una temporada en la que destacó con una séptima plaza en los 10.000 metros del Europeo de pista en Birmingham y recientemente en Atapuerca, donde firmó una brillante octava plaza, siendo el tercer mejor español en meta. Otro de los integrantes del equipo campeón en 2025 que vuelve a la preselección es Ilias Fifa, duodécimo en Lagoa y pieza importante del triunfo colectivo español. Completan el equipo Adrià Ceballos, que llega después de contribuir al histórico primer título absoluto masculino del ADA Calvià-Vistassol en el Campeonato de España de Campo a Través disputado en Atapuerca, y Miguel Ángel Chazarra, que afronta la cita tras una sólida temporada de campo a través que remató en Atapuerca hace pocos días siendo el segundo mejor español. El equipo absoluto femenino presenta una preselección liderada por Carolina Robles, que esta temporada dio el salto a la distancia de maratón en el Europeo de Birmingham. Consumada especialista en campo a través, la sevillana afrontará su séptimo Europeo de cross, en los que suma sendos decimosextos puestos en 2023 y 2024. Entre las atletas con mayor experiencia internacional figura Idaira Prieto, que disputará su sexto Europeo, tercero en categoría absoluta. La fondista fue decimoséptima en Lagoa 2025 y llega avalada por su cuarta posición en los 10.000 metros del Europeo de pista de Birmingham y por haber sido la segunda española en cruzar la meta en Atapuerca. Junto a ella estará Carla Gallardo, plusmarquista española de 10 km en ruta; María Forero, campeona de Europa sub-23 en Lagoa 2025 y primera española en conquistar el título continental de cross en dos categorías diferentes; y Marta Serrano, sexta en Lagoa y una de las integrantes del equipo que conquistó el bronce colectivo. Aparte, España también competirá en la categoría del relevo mixto con el objetivo de reencontrarse con el podio continental al que ya ha subido en cinco ocasiones: 2017 (bronce), 2018 (oro), 2019 (bronce), 2021 (bronce) y 2022 (plata). De cara a la cita de Belgrado, los atletas han participado en una concentración específica de monitorización del relevo mixto de campo a través, destinada a evaluar su rendimiento y definir la composición del equipo. Tras este proceso, el cuarteto español estará integrado por Mariano García, Martín Segurola, Marta Mitjans y Rocío Garrido. La preselección completa es la siguiente: · Absoluto masculino: Adrià Ceballos, Miguel Ángel Chazarra, Ilias Fifa, Rodrigue Kwizera*, Thierry Ndikumwenayo y Abdessamad Oukhelfen. * Siempre que World Athletics conceda a tiempo la autorización necesaria ·Absoluto femenino: María Forero, Carla Gallardo, Idaira Prieto, Carolina Robles, Marta Serrano y Ángela Viciosa. · Relevo mixto: Mariano García, Rocío Garrido, Marta Mitjans y Martín Segurola. · Sub23 masculino: Manex Cívico, Mesfin Escamilla, Óscar Gaitán, Rubén Leonardo, Pedro Viciosa, Aleix Vives. · Sub23 femenino: Candela Blázquez, Andrea Buenavida, Emma Méndez, Silvia Rey, Ámbar Tomàs y María Viciosa. · Sub20 masculino: Adrià Boyano, Teo de Frutos, Álvaro González, Alejandro Ibáñez, Alejandro Muñoz y Álex Sierpes. · Sub20 femenino: Rocío García, Sandra González, Claudia Gutiérrez, Debritu Paniagua, Demeku Paniagua y Mara Rolli

articles.title: London Museum: What's it like inside the new Smithfield Market venue?
articles.summary: The venue's new site at Smithfield Market opens on Saturday following a £437m restoration project.
articles.body:
Ten years ago the Museum of London announced it would be leaving its former home to move to the abandoned halls of Smithfield Market. Now rebranded London Museum, it is set to open its doors to the public on Saturday after a £437m project. So what's it like inside?

Leaning back on a leather sofa, museum director Sharon Ament looks across a vast brick-lined space that once bustled with market traders but is now filling with its newest visitors.

"I really love this space, it just makes me smile every time I come in - it's actually joyful," she says.

The vast room, now known as Our Time, is dotted with installations reflecting living memory.

In one corner a life-size mechanical giraffe flicks its ears in front of a lit-up NHS sign representing lockdown. Another wall has remnants of London's former greyhound tracks. Near it is the old switchboard from Buckingham Palace.

And beneath the magnificent domed ceiling roam several flocks of large plastic sheep which Ament encourages people to "pull up and take a seat" on.

"There are grins on people's faces, so I think we've pulled something rather incredible off," she says.

A visit to the new museum starts before this point as people enter through a large covered street known as Real Time.

Here, data-filled digital displays tell of London in the moment, beside a Banksy-graffitied sentry box and the last bell to be cast at the historic Whitechapel Bell Foundry .

Next they enter the former General Market with its sheep, giraffe and signage.

This is the space where events like late-night house parties and dinner clubs will be held beside shops and eateries, including former Victorian cocoa rooms that will be open 24 hours a day at weekends.

Such hints of the building's past are everywhere. Halfway up the walls are the restored fireplaces of the traders' former offices, along with twisting metal staircases that once led up to them.

"Whenever we've found historic fabric, we've restored it or kept it, and we want to show the layers of history," explains Alec Shaw, who has led the entire project.

"We wanted a museum that worked like the market, that allowed you to come in any corner and just walk across, walk through the building on your way to work, or, hopefully, stay a bit longer."

Shaw previously showed me around the site nearly three years ago , when scaffolding and supports were holding up the walls and there were constant splashes of water dripping on to the floor.

Restoring a Victorian relic that was abandoned in the 1990s "really tested all of us", he admits, and that was before the logistics involved in designing a new museum from the venue's seven-million object collection.

Five thousand of these are now on site and another 300,000 are due to arrive for when the former Poultry Market becomes a museum space in 2028.

"We think you could take at least eight hours to see every object downstairs, and that means you're going to keep coming back.

"The best museums are those that you go, 'Right I'll do that one today. I'll do this gallery next time,'" he says.

A wide staircase to one side descends into what is called Past Time.

Down here is what once was street level of Roman London, and curator Annette Day explains that "we felt that right in the guts, in the earth of the city, that was the place where we should explore London".

A weaving route beneath a seven-metre-high brick vaulted ceiling tells the capital's story.

It starts with the city's creation by the Romans and moves through medieval times and London's place as the centre of the British Empire, before ending with the 2012 Olympic Games, a time when "London looked at itself and the world looked at London", says Day.

Along the way are all manner of objects.

There's Charles I's execution vest, Queen Victoria's mourning dress, a white 1960s Ford Cortina, an overstuffed taxidermy cat called Oliver and the shimmering Elizabethan jewellery of the Cheapside Hoard.

Galleries on either side also focus on specific moments.

One features a recreated Roman room with amphoras - two-handled jars - a mosaic floor and the pieces of a magnificent wall painting found in Lime Street 20 years ago that hang on the wall.

Another uses large comic illustrations based on new research to tell the story of the Great Fire of London in an attempt to reflect the subject's inclusion in Key Stage 1 of the national curriculum.

Further along still, two other archways branch off to look at the lives of Londoners and the city's landscape, placing objects from across the ages alongside each other.

The delicately feathered Dying Swan outfit worn by lauded Russian dancer Anna Pavlova stands beside the stage outfit of Edwardian music hall star Kitty Lord in one case, while another shows 2,000 years of London-made shoes.

One case is even filled with toilets and chamber pots from medieval times to today.

And to carry on that subject, on the far wall a small porthole frames a chunk of the eponymous Whitechapel fatberg , not far from the huge glass window that looks out on passing Thameslink trains (whose passengers apparently are yet to notice they are now being watched).

Even with its planned events, shops and eateries, Ament says it is all these objects which remain "the essence of the museum" because they "tell stories in a compelling way".

She sees the museum as a shared space for everyone, somewhere for Londoners and tourists alike to connect with people and stories from the past and now.

"Think of this as like one of my favourite buses, the number 63 bus. You meet the world on it. And you meet the world in here."

Most important of all, she says, is that the London Museum must always represent and reflect the city it is in.

"The story of London is tough and joyful at the same time. That's why we use 'grit and glitter' as a tagline - it's both of those things, those dualities can exist. And we shouldn't be frightened of that history," she says.

"We are making a museum and it will never stop, just like London never stops. There's always cranes in London and there'll always be new things in London Museum."

articles.title: BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships: Amid personal loss, Priya Sheoran hopes to make her mark
articles.summary: The past few months have tested Priya Sheoran in ways far beyond the athletics field.
articles.body: The past few months have tested Priya Sheoran in ways far beyond the athletics field.The Haryana discus thrower had been making frequent trips to hospital as her father Anup, a sub-inspector with Haryana Police and the man who inspired her to take up sports, had been unwell for several months. He passed away on Nov 10.Barely a fortnight later, Priya is set to step into the competition arena again, carrying both the grief of her loss and the hope of putting up a strong performance at the three-day inaugural BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships to be held at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar from Wednesday.“For the past four months, I had been going back and forth to the hospital with him. So, the preparation hasn’t been that good, but let’s hope for the best,” said Priya.The youngster, who has trained under celebrated discus thrower Seema Punia, won bronze at the U23 Asian Athletics Championships earlier this year, her first international medal.“It felt really good because it was my first international medal. This tournament is also being organised for the first time, so I’ll try to perform well here too and hopefully win a medal,” said the 22-year-old.Given what she has been through in recent months, Priya is trying not to burden herself with expectations. “I just want to put my best foot forward and give my best. I haven’t really thought about the result yet. I’ll go in with the mindset that I have to perform well,” she added.Priya will be among a 70-member Indian contingent looking to make an impression at the event.A little more than 200 athletes from six countries are expected to compete in the three-day event. With Thailand pulling out, athletes from Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Nepal and Sri Lanka will join hosts India in the competition.Among those attracting attention will also be 17-year-old sprinter Neil Samraj, who comes into the event on the back of a record-breaking season.Samraj broke the U18 national record in the 100m twice in a single day at the National Youth Athletics Championships in Ludhiana, eventually clocking 10.46s in the final. He lowered the mark further at the National Junior Athletics Championships in Chennai last month, running 10.45s. He also rewrote the U18 national record in the 200m in Chennai with a time of 21.03 seconds.Now, with an opportunity to test himself against athletes from the region, Samraj wants to see where he stands at the end of a long season.“Competing internationally will help me gain experience and prepare for many more international competitions where I will be up against athletes from different countries,” Samraj said in a social media post released by the Athletics Federation of India.“The plan is just to go hard because this is a very good opportunity to participate in a regional international competition. It will also help me understand where I stand and what kind of timings I can produce towards the end of the season.”For India’s young athletes, the championships provide another international opportunity at the end of a season that has witnessed several national records tumble. For Priya, however, simply returning to the throwing circle after a difficult few months will carry a significance of its own.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: España, campeona de las Series Mundiales de natación paralímpica
articles.standfirst: Teresa Perales ha sido segunda de la general individual y campeona de las clases bajas y la almeriense Tasy Dmytriv campeona júnior
articles.summary: Teresa Perales ha sido segunda de la general individual y campeona de las clases bajas y la almeriense Tasy Dmytriv campeona júnior
articles.body: España se ha proclamado campeona de las Series Mundiales de natación paralímpica por primera vez en la historia, tras la conclusión de un circuito en el que la aragonesa Teresa Perales ha sido segunda de la general individual y campeona de las clases bajas y la almeriense Tasy Dmytriv campeona júnior. Una vez concluido el circuito de las Series Mundiales, la organización ha publicado las clasificaciones finales del circuito 2026, coronando a España como campeona de los 52 países en competición con 15.390 puntos por delante de Estados Unidos, Francia, Países Bajos y Brasil. Las cuatro puntuaciones que construyen el resultado de España están impulsadas por cuatro nadadores de la Federación Española de Deportes de Personas con Discapacidad Física (FEDDF) como Teresa Perales (4.002), Tasy Dmytriv (3.744), Toni Ponce (3.940) e Íñigo Llopis (3.704). La clasificación individual refleja que Teresa Perales es subcampeona de la clasificación general femenina entre 478 nadadoras de todas las clases y, además, campeona de la categoría de clases bajas S/SB1-3. La almeriense Tasy Dmytriv terminó novena del mundo en la clasificación general femenina y además es campeona de las Series Mundiales Júnior 2026. Entre las españolas resalta el resultado de Catalina Sagastizabal, que, con apenas 16 años, termina décima del 'ranking' mundial júnior entre 143 nadadoras. Entre los hombres también hay presencia entre los mejores del circuito de Toni Ponce, sexto del mundo entre 680 nadadores; Iñigo Llopis, decimoctavo, y Jacobo Garrido, vigésimo.

articles.title: Indian Women's Hockey team creates history, storms to world no. 4 after 4-0 win over Japan
articles.summary: From breaking into the top five to reaching an unprecedented fourth spot in just 24 hours, the Indian women's hockey team is rewriting its place in the
articles.body: From breaking into the top five to reaching an unprecedented fourth spot in just 24 hours, the Indian women's hockey team is rewriting its place in the international game. A commanding 4-0 victory over Japan in the Women's Asian Champions Trophy 2026 on Wednesday propelled India to World No. 4 in the latest FIH World Rankings, marking the highest position achieved by the team in its history.The latest milestone came just a day after India had entered the top five for the first time, climbing to fifth following an emphatic 6-2 victory over China at the International Sports Complex in Nathu Barkheda. Back-to-back wins over two of Asia's strongest teams helped the defending champions make another significant leap in the rankings.The victory over Japan also extended India's unbeaten run in the tournament to five matches, ensuring a perfect league-stage record and a place in the semi-finals.India dominate China and Japan to reach historic rankingIndia's 6-2 triumph over China was particularly significant as it marked the team's biggest-ever victory against the Chinese side in the history of the Women's Asian Champions Trophy. The previous best was a 4-2 win in the 2013 edition.The team followed that performance with another dominant display against Japan, securing a comfortable 4-0 victory.With victories over Malaysia, Thailand, South Korea, China and Japan, the Indian team has enjoyed an impressive campaign under captain Salima Tete.India's journey to its highest-ever FIH rankingIndia's rise to World No. 4 marks a major milestone in the team's international journey since the introduction of the FIH World Rankings in October 2003. Before this achievement, the team's best ranking was sixth, which it reached in May-June 2022 following an impressive FIH Pro League campaign. India also attained the sixth position in 2023.The team had previously climbed to World No. 8 after finishing fourth at the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games and reached ninth in 2018 following its quarter-final appearance at the Hockey World Cup. The latest jump to fourth reflects the progress Indian women's hockey has made over the years and its growing presence among the leading teams in international competition.India's rise in the FIH rankings adds another major achievement to an outstanding year for the team. The side won the FIH Nations Cup, secured a historic fifth-place finish at the FIH Hockey World Cup — its best-ever performance at the tournament since 1974 — and claimed the Asian Games gold medal after a gap of 44 years.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Three Nations Cup: GB, France & Germany launch new swimming competition
articles.summary: Aquatics GB organises a new Three Nations Cup event alongside France and Germany, saying it is time for "elite swimming competition to evolve".
articles.body:
Aquatics GB has organised a new competition called the Three Nations Cup alongside France and Germany, saying it is time for "elite swimming competition to evolve".

The annual series will host 22 races in 90 minutes, with the first event taking place in Manchester on Sunday, 14 March 2027, before moving to Paris on Sunday, 21 March.

The aim is to modernise elite swimming and introduce new audiences to the excitement of international racing, the governing body says.

Mixed relays will sit alongside women's and men's 50m 'skins' races in butterfly, backstroke and breaststroke.

The skins races - a name for elimination-style swimming - will see six swimmers reduced to four and then two across three rounds.

"It is time for elite swimming competition to evolve. Together with our counterparts in France and Germany, we have created a series that puts the excitement of racing at its heart," Aquatics GB chief Drew Barrand said.

"We want fans to feel the pressure of every race. With elimination rounds, mixed relays and points carrying across two weekends, the Three Nations Cup gives them a fast-paced team contest to get behind from the first start to the final touch."

Points will be awarded across both legs, with the team at the top of the standings after Paris winning the Three Nations Cup and the prize-money pot.

Spectators will also draw the swimming order for the mixed 4x200m freestyle relay, adding another twist to the team contest.

Broadcast details and athlete selections for all three countries will be announced in due course.

"France, Germany and Great Britain have developed this series together. We look forward to welcoming the teams and their supporters to Paris for the deciding meet," president of the French Swimming Federation Gilles Sezionale added.

Christian Hansmann, head of performance at the German Swimming Federation, added: "As sporting rivals, we each want to win. As partners, we share the goal of bringing more people into swimming's audience. The Three Nations Cup makes both possible."

articles.title: India to make 2036 Olympics bid presentation today: Focus on infrastructure, sustainable projects
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India will make its case to host the 2036 Summer Olympics and Paralympics on Thursday in a virtual session before the International Olympic
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India will make its case to host the 2036 Summer Olympics and Paralympics on Thursday in a virtual session before the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) Future Host Commission. India hopes to impress the IOC's board with a strong infrastructure model in Ahmedabad and a strong past record of conducting global events.India is one of the seven countries that will be making these presentations over a two-day period. Germany, Hungary, Qatar, South Korea, South Africa and Turkiye are the other countries that have shown interest in hosting the 2036 Games.India's case, to be made from an office in New Delhi, will be represented by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Sports Secretary Hari Ranjan Rao, outgoing Indian Olympic Association (IOA) President PT Usha, IOA Athletes Commission head PV Sindhu, Gujarat Sports Minister Harsh Sanghavi, IOA CEO Raghuram Iyer and IOC member Nita Ambani.During the presentations, each country's case will be assessed on the basis of its infrastructure preparations, sustainable projects, legacy and viability to host the Olympics and Paralympics.India is expected to stress its capacity to host multiple big-ticket tournaments in the past. Additionally, with Ahmedabad due to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games, most of the venues and infrastructure will be ready in Gujarat.India hosted 36 international events across more than 15 cities between January 2025 and June 2026. Over the next two years (2027 and 2028), India is set to host another 19 international sporting competitions.After the presentation on Thursday, the IOC will carry out an "anonymous survey" to gauge public sentiment towards India's bid.The survey is likely to take place in the third week of December and will factor into the assessment of India's bid in March next year. That evaluation will be followed by the Strategic Dialogue phase, in which interested nations will be required to submit their preliminary responses to the Future Host Questionnaire along with core financial guarantees.The final stage of the decision-making process, the Targeted Dialogue, is set to begin in 2028, when IOC Members will be presented with a report by the Future Host Commission.Subsequently, in mid-2029, the IOC Executive Board will name the Preferred Hosts to be "proposed for election by the IOC Session as the host of the 2036 Olympic Games."Last month, the IOC had invited all seven interested countries to present their Games proposals to the Future Host Commission.The IOC chief Kirsty Coventry-headed panel said the bids would be evaluated on several technical criteria, including the venue master plan and athlete experience, funding model, political and public backing, Games delivery capability, and legacy plans aimed at ensuring lasting benefits for host communities.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
